# On Intentionalism
There's a mathematical insight that explains why some people consistently end up with better outcomes than others, and it has nothing to do with talent, luck, or even the quality of their choices.
And when systems have this structure, even roughly, we should expect to see the same pattern—proposers systematically getting better outcomes than receivers.
And proposers—whether in the pure mathematics of matching algorithms or in the messy approximations of real life—end up with better outcomes.

nodes.text: In 1962, David Gale and Lloyd Shapley worked on creating stable pairings, where no two unmatched people would prefer each other over their assigned partners.

evidence.text:
## The Setup
In 1962, mathematician-economists David Gale and Lloyd Shapley were working on a problem about how to create stable pairings between two groups of people. Their goal was to prove whether you could always match everyone in a way where no two unmatched people would prefer each other over their assigned partners.

nodes.text: They proved you could always match everyone this way, and presented an algorithm to find such matchings.

evidence.text: They proved you could, and presented an algorithm to find such matchings. But in analyzing their algorithm, they discovered something remarkable about the structure of who proposes and who responds.

nodes.text: In their deferred acceptance algorithm, one side makes proposals in order of preference, and the other accepts or tentatively rejects.

evidence.text: In their "deferred acceptance" algorithm, one side makes proposals in order of preference, and the other side accepts or tentatively rejects based on their preferences. When they analyzed what this produces, they found that proposers get their best possible partner among all stable (mutually acceptable) matchings, while receivers get their worst possible partner among all stable matchings.

nodes.text: Proposers get their best possible partner among all stable matchings, while receivers get their worst possible partner.

evidence.text: In their "deferred acceptance" algorithm, one side makes proposals in order of preference, and the other side accepts or tentatively rejects based on their preferences. When they analyzed what this produces, they found that proposers get their best possible partner among all stable (mutually acceptable) matchings, while receivers get their worst possible partner among all stable matchings.

nodes.text: This is not slightly better or worse: it is systematically, provably, mathematically extreme for each individual.

evidence.text: This isn't just slightly better or worse—it's systematically, provably, mathematically extreme. In the specific algorithm they designed, each individual proposer ends up with the best stable partner they could possibly get, and each individual receiver ends up with the worst stable partner they could possibly have.

nodes.text: Real-world situations share the proposer-receiver structure, even roughly, so the same pattern should appear.

evidence.text:
## Why This Matters Beyond Mathematics
Now, most real-world situations don't follow the exact Gale-Shapley algorithm. But they share the fundamental structure: one side proposes or initiates, and the other side responds or selects from what's offered.
And when systems have this structure, even roughly, we should expect to see the same pattern—proposers systematically getting better outcomes than receivers.

nodes.text: Four everyday choices show the default: deciding what you want versus choosing among what is offered.

evidence.text: Think about how most of your choices actually happen:

nodes.text: Netflix: scrolling through recommendations until something looks good enough, rather than deciding what kind of experience you wanted.

evidence.text: Before you opened Netflix tonight, did you decide what kind of experience you wanted? Or did you scroll through recommendations until something looked good enough?

nodes.text: Phone: choosing among what was prominently displayed, rather than researching what features you actually needed.

evidence.text: When you bought your last phone, did you research what features you actually needed? Or did you choose among what was prominently displayed at the store?

nodes.text: Job: applying to positions that happened to be posted, rather than pursuing companies doing work you cared about.

evidence.text: That job you have—did you identify companies doing work you cared about and pursue them? Or did you apply to positions that happened to be posted?

nodes.text: Friendship: accepting a connection that formed through proximity or circumstance, rather than seeking out someone with qualities you value.

evidence.text: The friend you're meeting for coffee—did you seek out someone with qualities you value? Or did you accept a connection that formed through proximity or circumstance?

nodes.text: For most of these, most of us are receivers: choosing from what is presented, not pursuing what we want intentionally.

evidence.text: For most of these, most of us are receivers. We're choosing from what's presented, not pursuing what we want intentionally. And while these situations aren't running the Gale-Shapley algorithm exactly, they have the same basic structure—one side initiates (proposes), the other responds (receives).

nodes.text: The insidious thing is not terrible outcomes; receivers get acceptable, good enough ones: a decent show, a functional phone, a reasonable job, pleasant friendships.

evidence.text:
## The Pattern in Practice
The insidious thing about being a receiver isn't that you get terrible outcomes. You don't. You get acceptable ones. Good enough ones. You watch a decent show, buy a functional phone, work a reasonable job, have pleasant friendships.

nodes.text: But decent is not the same as what would actually serve you best.

evidence.text: But "decent" isn't the same as "what would actually serve you best."

nodes.text: Outcomes tend to favor whoever is doing the proposing, not because of a conspiracy but because the structure itself creates the advantage.

evidence.text: When systems operate on a proposer-receiver structure, even informally, the outcomes tend to favor whoever's doing the proposing. Not because of some conspiracy, but because of the mathematical properties that Gale and Shapley identified in their algorithm. The structure itself creates the advantage.

nodes.text: The system is self-sustaining precisely because it does not screw you badly enough to make you revolt.

evidence.text: Here's what makes it worse: because your outcomes feel fine, you never develop the dissatisfaction that would push you to become a proposer. The system is stable (self-sustaining) precisely because it doesn't screw you badly enough to make you revolt. It just quietly, consistently ensures you get less than you could have if you were on the other side of the equation.

## The Chicken and Egg
To be a proposer, you need to know what you want—you need intention. But if you've spent your whole life as a receiver, how would you know?
This is the trap. You need intention to propose, but you develop intention through proposing.

nodes.text: Intention and initiative build progressively, like a muscle.

evidence.text:
## The Training Ground
You can't jump straight from "I pick from what Netflix recommends" to "I have a clear vision for my life's work." The muscle of intention and initiative builds progressively.

evidence.text:
## The Training Ground
You can't jump straight from "I pick from what Netflix recommends" to "I have a clear vision for my life's work." The muscle of intention and initiative builds progressively.

nodes.text: Start tonight: before opening any app, decide what you actually want from the next hour, specifically whether to laugh, learn, feel calm, or be challenged.

evidence.text: Start small. Tonight, before opening any app, decide intentionally what you actually want from the next hour. Not "something entertaining" but specifically: do you want to laugh? Learn something? Feel calm? Be challenged?

nodes.text: Then pursue that intentionally: do not open Netflix and see what it suggests, do not scroll TikTok until something catches you.

evidence.text: Then pursue that intentionally. Don't open Netflix and see what it suggests. Don't scroll TikTok until something catches you. Actively seek what you decided you wanted.

nodes.text: The practice is not about one evening; it rebuilds the capacity to intend and then act on that intention.

evidence.text: The practice isn't about that one evening's entertainment. It's about rebuilding the capacity to intend and then act on that intention. Do this enough times, and you start to notice patterns in what satisfies you. Those patterns become preferences. Those preferences become values.

Think about the last time you made a major life decision. Getting married, taking a job, moving to a city, choosing what to study.

## The Collective Effect
This isn't just about individual outcomes. When most people are receivers, entire systems shift to optimize for whoever's doing the proposing.

nodes.text: Companies build for what they can convince people to want among presented options, not for what people need.

evidence.text: Companies don't build products for what people need—they build for what they can convince people to want among presented options. Dating apps don't facilitate people finding compatible partners—they optimize for engagement among available profiles. Content platforms don't serve what would genuinely satisfy you—they test what keeps you scrolling among suggested posts.

The structural disadvantage of being a receiver doesn't go away because you understand it. You have to actually switch positions.
